content: The angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptors in the endocrine pancreas act as an entry point for the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), the virus responsible for COVID-19. Researchers in China have observed cases of new-onset diabetes in patients infected with SARS-CoV, suggesting that SARS-CoV-2 may similarly invade pancreatic islet cells by binding to ACE2 receptors. This interaction can result in acute β-cell injury, leading to severe hyperglycemia and transient Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM). SARS-CoV-2 can induce hyperglycemia both by directly damaging pancreatic beta cells and by downregulating ACE2 receptors, which leads to unopposed angiotensin II activity, potentially impairing insulin secretion. A case report described a previously healthy patient who developed diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) triggered by COVID-19. The patient presented with a one-week history of fever (38.5°C), vomiting, polydipsia (excessive thirst), and polyuria (excessive urination). Initial treatment included 6 liters of intravenous fluids and an intravenous insulin infusion over 24 hours. The DKA resolved the following day, and the patient transitioned to subcutaneous insulin therapy. Diabetes mellitus encompasses a range of conditions characterized by insulin deficiency, either due to reduced insulin secretion or resistance at the target organs. These include Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM), Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM), gestational diabetes, and maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY). T1DM is caused by autoimmune destruction or failure of pancreatic β-cells and typically presents in children and young adults. T2DM, on the other hand, is associated with insulin resistance and is more common in adults, with risk factors including family history, obesity, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. Globally, approximately 422 million people have diabetes, with the majority residing in lowand middle-income countries. Diabetes is directly responsible for 1.6 million deaths annually, and its prevalence has been steadily increasing over recent decades. In a 2008 study conducted in China, researchers compared 39 SARS-CoV patients without prior diabetes to 39 healthy siblings. Among the SARS-CoV patients, 20 developed new-onset diabetes during hospitalization. However, three years post-recovery, only 5% of these patients remained diabetic, with the majority experiencing normalization of blood glucose levels. ACE2 is the primary receptor for the spike protein of both SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2. These viruses infect cells by binding to ACE2 receptors. Evidence suggests that SARS-CoV may damage pancreatic islets, leading to acute insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus. In April 2020, an 18-year-old German student, Finn Gnadt, was diagnosed with T1DM shortly after recovering from SARS-CoV-2 infection. His physician hypothesized that the virus had destroyed his β-cells, as his blood lacked the immune cells typically associated with autoimmune β-cell destruction. There is currently no established classification system for COVID-19-associated diabetes. Further research is needed to determine whether SARS-CoV-2 induces T1DM, T2DM, or a novel form of diabetes. The pathophysiology of COVID-19-associated diabetes involves ACE2 receptors, which are expressed in metabolically active tissues such as pancreatic beta cells, adipose tissue, the small intestine, and the kidneys. Pancreatic cells, including beta and alpha cells, express both ACE2 and the effector protease TMPRSS2, making them susceptible to SARS-CoV-2 infection. Immunohistochemical studies have confirmed the presence of ACE2 in pancreatic islet cells, with both insulin-secreting beta cells and glucagon-secreting alpha cells testing positive for the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. This suggests that the virus can directly infect pancreatic islet cells. Experimental studies using human pluripotent stem cell-derived pancreatic endocrine cells have shown that SARS-CoV-2 infection disrupts key metabolic pathways, including calcium signaling and glucagon signaling in alpha cells, as well as insulin secretion pathways in beta cells. Infected cells exhibit increased apoptosis, as evidenced by staining with the apoptotic marker CASP3. This indicates that SARS-CoV-2-induced metabolic dysfunction in the pancreas is primarily driven by cell death. ACE2 serves as a negative regulator of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS), converting angiotensin I and II into their less active forms, Ang 1-9 and Ang 1-7. When SARS-CoV-2 binds to ACE2, it downregulates ACE2 expression, disrupting this protective pathway. This shifts the balance toward the ACE/Ang II/AT1R axis, which promotes oxidative stress, inflammation, and fibrosis in pancreatic islets, impairing insulin secretion and increasing the risk of diabetes. Experimental studies have shown that angiotensin II suppresses insulin release, contributing to the development of T2DM. The exact mechanisms by which SARS-CoV-2 causes diabetes remain under investigation. However, two primary pathways have been proposed: direct damage to pancreatic beta cells and ACE2 downregulation, which shifts the RAS balance toward harmful pathways. The natural history of hyperglycemia includes symptoms such as blurry vision, excessive thirst, fatigue, frequent urination, hunger, and weight loss. While data on the prognosis of COVID-19-associated diabetes is limited, studies on SARS-CoV suggest that most cases of new-onset diabetes resolve after recovery from the infection. The diagnostic gold standard for diabetes mellitus is fasting plasma glucose (FPG), with a threshold of ≥126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) according to the American Diabetes Association (ADA). Other diagnostic tests include HbA1C and random plasma glucose (RPG). Treatment for COVID-19-associated diabetes includes managing hyperglycemia and complications such as DKA. In one case, a patient received intravenous fluids and insulin infusion, followed by subcutaneous insulin therapy. Surgical interventions are not recommended for this condition. Primary prevention strategies for diabetes include maintaining a healthy weight and active lifestyle.
